1:
Ellicott states the complaint the verse answers: Moses had charged God with delay, with being slack concerning his promise, and with not delivering his people at all; now shalt thou see assures him there will be no more delay — the work is about to begin, he will behold it, and will then cease to doubt. Calvin hears something sharper in the same phrase, a tacit reproof of an impatience that would not wait for the result of the promise; and he thinks Moses unworthy of so kind a reply, the Father of all goodness pardoning the sins of leader and people alike that he might effect the deliverance he had determined. Henry fixes the moment: Moses was at his wit's end, wishing he had stayed in Midian rather than come to Egypt to make bad worse, and now that the affair had come to a crisis, Pharaoh at the height of pride and Israel in the depth of misery, it was God's time to appear — man's extremity being God's opportunity, and the church's deliverance accomplished when God takes the work into his own hands. Gill notes only that the word answered the questions and expostulations Moses had put.

On the strong hand Clarke observes that the Hebrew uses the verb elsewhere translated to harden, and takes it for sovereign power suddenly and forcibly applied: God would display his power before the Egyptians, and Pharaoh in consequence would display his own by thrusting the people out. Ellicott would render through a strong hand rather than with it, the compulsion God exerts. Calvin explains why God refused a voluntary release: he wished the work of liberation to be conspicuous, and drive them out is to be pressed — the king who today refuses will not merely consent but expel them from his kingdom, counting their speed a blessing. Henry turns the phrase to use: as some are brought to their duty by the strong hand of grace, made willing in the day of God's power, so others by the strong hand of justice, which breaks those that will not bend.

Henry files his account of the whole message here, finding five grounds of comfort in it. The first is the name: I am Jehovah is one with I am that I am, the fountain of being and infinite perfection, a God who performs what he has promised, so inviting confidence in them, and who perfects what he has begun. He observes that in the creation history God is never called Jehovah until the heavens and the earth were finished; meanwhile his people find him El-shaddai, a God all-sufficient. The second is the covenant, for the covenants God makes he also establishes, as firm as his power and truth can make them, so we may venture our all upon that bottom. The third is his compassion, since he notices the increase of his people's calamities and how their enemies grow upon them.

The fourth is the resolutions themselves, line upon line — I will bring out, I will rid, I will redeem, I will bring in, I will give — where man may take the shame of an unbelief needing such repetition and God the glory of the condescending grace that grants it. The fifth is the intention behind them, double: their happiness, in being taken for a peculiar people and having him for their God, than which we cannot have more; and his own glory, that they should know him the Lord — for God will attain his own ends, nor shall we come short of them if we make them our chief end too. That such words did not revive them he accounts for three ways: they were too taken up with their troubles to heed Moses, too cast down by the late disappointment to believe him, and too afraid of Pharaoh's wrath to stir towards their own deliverance.
2:
Gill takes the declaration for a summary of the divine nature: the self-existent Being, the everlasting I am, unchangeable and constant to his promises. Clarke insists the rendering should be I am Jehovah, since without the proper name the next verse's reason is not obvious; Wesley glosses it as a God who gives being to his own promises. Calvin reads the speech as a rebuke of distrust by way of the covenant. God advances nothing new, since the people had almost imbibed the doctrine of their adoption with their mother's milk; so their complaint against Moses, as though he had invented what he promised in God's name, is less pardonable. The comparison stings: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob embraced the promise and trusted it perseveringly, while their descendants disdained it because fulfilment did not appear at once.

On the older name they are close. Gill makes El-shaddai God all-sufficient, having a sufficiency of happiness in himself and enough for his creatures' wants; Clarke renders it the dispenser or pourer-out of gifts. Ellicott traces it from Abraham through Isaac to Jacob, finding its primary idea in overpowering strength, against which the idea of Jehovah is absolute, eternal, unconditional existence. Calvin canvasses the etymologies without settling them, and holds that where God engages himself to Abraham under it he promises to be merciful and bounteous, the respect being to loving-kindness rather than might in judgment.

The denial that the fathers knew the name Jehovah Clarke calls a crux, since it occurs from Genesis onward and God had used it of himself to Abraham. He canvasses four solutions: that the sentence be read as a question, the negative particle often having that force; that the name was first revealed here and used earlier by anticipation; that since it signifies existence, God is now giving existence to the promises; and that the words are comparative, the fathers knowing the name but not the power now to be shown. His own answer is that the name was known from the first but what it implied was not — a man may bear the title of an office long before he does any of its work, king, magistrate and constable being known for what they are only by their acts. Ellicott renders it was I not made manifest to them, and defends its antiquity from a derivation out of a form already obsolete in Moses' day, from its presence in the oldest documents taken up into Genesis, and from Abraham's use of it in a place-name. Why the stress shifted he explains historically: the patriarchs needed assurance that God could perform, whereas Israel stood in closest contact with polytheism and had partly fallen into it, the Existent meaning the Self-Existent and so the Only Existent, a standing protest against every other god.

Gill holds the covenant sure and never to be made null; Clarke has God now fully purposed to give effect to all his engagements. Ellicott renders the next phrase the land of their sojournings wherein they sojourned, Canaan having been occupied by sufferance, the ownership reckoned the Canaanites'. Calvin makes that tolerance their praise: it was exemplary virtue to wander all their lives with no corner to set a foot on but what neighbours allowed for a tent, in a land the covenant had made their inheritance — which condemns the posterity who would not go up to it. He explains the long delay too: God would have them sorely troubled that he might succour them more openly, and unjustly oppressed that he might rescue them the more justly — had the laws of hospitality been kept, there had been no cause to shake off the yoke. Gill adds that he sympathises in their afflictions and notices their sighs; Wesley refers the groaning to the late hardships; and Calvin notes that God's remembering means the showing of it by what he does.
6:
Gill grounds the promises in the name that heads them: eternal in being, immutable in counsel, faithful to his covenant and able to fulfil it. Ellicott notices that the idea of God redeeming Israel appears here first, and that the redemption was accomplished twice over — by the wonders culminating in the tenth plague, whereby they ceased to be Pharaoh's slaves and became God's servants, and by the passage of the Red Sea, which delivered them from death and so purchased them anew. Wesley reads the stretched-out arm as almighty power, a metaphor from a man stretching his arm out to put forth all his strength.

Gill explains the taking of a people two ways: politically, that out of Egyptian hands they should be his kingdom and subjects, and religiously, that they should be a holy people to fear and serve him by rules given from himself — both effected by setting up a civil and an ecclesiastical polity. Clarke identifies the promise as the covenant made with Abraham, then asks why God should take so refractory and worthless a people for his own. He answers three ways: because he had promised their ancestors, in general friends of God; because, as Warburton observes, the providence protecting them was the more visible for their want of shining qualities, which might otherwise have let the effects be ascribed to their own wisdom; and because God would show that he delights to save the lost, choosing the worst people in the universe to prove that he wills not the death of a sinner. Ellicott guards the other side: the choice of a peculiar people did not mean abandoning the rest, since God continued to govern all nations and in every nation accepted those who feared him — a principle the centurion and Cornelius carry into the Gospel.

Calvin presses the promise past the departure. It would have been little that the people should once be redeemed unless they then lived under God's guardianship; having long since set the holy seed apart by circumcision he sets it apart again, so that both their election and its perpetuity are asserted — to be accounted God's people being to be received by special privilege into his favour and called by adoption to the hope of eternal salvation. Canaan he treats as the earnest of that adoption, the fathers' faith not being tied to earthly blessings. On the lifting up of the hand he and Clarke agree that it is the gesture of an oath, which Calvin adds cannot properly be said of God, who swears by himself because there is none greater, and that there is more than enough steadfastness in his simple word, the oath a concession to human weakness.

Why the message failed is answered together. Ellicott contrasts the two announcements: at the first they believed and worshipped, their spirits springing to a hope they had long been strangers to, but by now they had been chilled by disappointment, their leader's interference having only increased their misery. Keil fixes the Hebrew closely: it is shortness of breath, meaning not impatience but anguish, an inward pressure that stops a man breathing properly — the early belief changed into the despondency of unbelief as the oppression grew, and it spread to Moses, who declined his commission again. Clarke says their labour was so continual and their bondage so cruel they had scarcely time to breathe, and notes that the Samaritan adds a sentence here, let us alone that we may serve the Egyptians, borrowed from a later chapter. Calvin finds it marvellous rather than natural: no wonder men intoxicated with prosperity reject God's mercy, but sorrow ought to awaken longing, and instead the afflicted harden against the promises — so we should struggle to get our minds clear enough of grief to receive grace, there being no greater curse than being made too dull to hear.
10:
Gill has the orders renewed at another time, and remarks that access to Pharaoh seems not to have been difficult. Henry, whom Wesley abridges here, draws the rule that God repeats his precepts before he begins his punishments: those called in vain to leave their sins must be called again and again, whether they will hear or forbear, God being said to hew sinners by his prophets, which denotes the repetition of the strokes. Ellicott notices that the second message advances on the first: the first asked only leave to go into the wilderness, much of which lay within Egypt's limits, the second that Israel be let go out of the land. Such, he says, is the way of Providence: refuse a light cross and a heavier is laid on; decline the Sibyl's first offer and she brings a worse bargain the second time.

Calvin measures the forbearance in the renewal. The just reward of so malevolent a repulse would have been to let the people rot in their miseries; it is of God's extraordinary loving-kindness that he does not cease helping those willing to perish. The new command was needed to strengthen Moses, shaken by the people's despair and concluding he was to go no further. His objection Calvin sets out as an argument from the less to the greater: it would be harder to move Pharaoh against his will than to persuade the afflicted to accept help offered from heaven, and if the people's hearts were a closed door, why try to shift the exceeding great rock? So the heartiest of God's servants faint midway, where the path proves worse than they expected.

Henry finds two pleas in it. The first is the unlikelihood of Pharaoh's hearing: if the anguish of their spirit makes Israel deaf to what would comfort them, much more will pride make him deaf to what can only exasperate him — and if God's professing people will not hear his messengers, how shall his professed enemy? The second is the infirmity of speech, already sufficiently answered, so Moses ought not to have pressed it, the sufficiency of grace supplying nature's defects. Clarke takes the word rendered uncircumcised to signify anything exuberant or superfluous, and would have rendered it protuberant lips had Moses not been remarkable for his beauty; as it is he refers it to a want of ready utterance, from a defect in the organs of speech or a knowledge of Egyptian impaired by forty years away. Ellicott reports Rosenmüller's argument from the phrase that Moses was tongue-tied, but doubts more is meant than the slowness of speech alleged earlier: uncircumcised stands by Hebrew idiom for any imperfection interfering with efficiency, an uncircumcised ear being one that cannot hearken, an uncircumcised heart one that fails to understand.

Gill observes that the objection is passed over, having been sufficiently answered before, and Aaron joined in the charge. Henry reads that as God ending the dispute by interposing his own authority: when Moses repeats his baffled arguments he is argued with no longer but charged upon his allegiance, God's authority sufficing to answer all objections and binding men to obey without murmuring or disputing. Its place divides them. Keil takes it for a concluding summary preparing for the genealogy headed in the next verse, and cites Ranke as having proved its organic connection with the narrative so conclusively that even Knobel gave up the fragmentary hypothesis. Ellicott makes it a seam: the details stand at the opening of the next chapter, which he thinks originally followed the objection directly, this verse being added to summarise them when the genealogy was inserted. Calvin looks the other way, rendering the Lord had spoken and referring it back to the calling's commencement, to show that Moses and Aaron had not acted rashly but on command, and that however often the work was interrupted God's purpose held.
14:
Why a pedigree stands here they answer alike. Henry calls it no endless genealogy of the kind the apostle condemns, since it ends in Moses and Aaron and shows them Israelites, bone of the bone of those they were sent to deliver, raised up of their brethren as Christ also should be. Clarke makes it a proof that the two came in a direct line from Abraham, and calls the whole passage a parenthesis that does not belong to the narration. Calvin puts it more sharply: the leader's origin is testified to all ages so none may doubt the promise to Abraham was fulfilled in the departure, since under any other leader it might have been questioned who the chief author was; and because Satan has obscured this history through profane writers, labouring to bury the race of Abraham, Moses anticipates him by naming the heads of families. Ellicott sets it in its culture, genealogies holding as prominent a place among Arabians as among Jews, a would-be leader's descent being matter of curiosity to all who submitted to him.

The choice of three tribes divides them. Lightfoot, whom Henry reports, thought the three dignified here because their dying father had left them under marks of infamy, Reuben for his incest and the other two for the murder of the Shechemites, so that Moses would magnify God's mercy in their repentance; Gill gives the same opinion, that they were not rejected though rather cursed than blessed by Jacob. Both prefer the plainer account, that the first two are named for the third's sake, that order might be kept and the deliverers of Israel plainly appear Israelites. Keil explains the form: a father's-house is a technical term for a body of families called by a common ancestor, and the list begins at Reuben to fix Levi's place, naming only such sons of the first two as founded families.

On the ages Henry and Wesley agree — Levi a hundred and thirty-seven, Kohath a hundred and thirty-three, Amram a hundred and thirty-seven — and observe that Moses came far short of them and fixed seventy or eighty for the ordinary stretch of life; for now that Israel was a great nation and revelation was written rather than trusted to tradition, the two great reasons for the patriarchs' long lives had ceased. Clarke adds from Dodd that Levi is thought to have outlived all Jacob's sons, surviving Joseph by twenty-seven years though much the elder; and he finds the promise of deliverance in the fourth generation verified exactly, Moses being son of Amram, son of Kohath, son of Levi, son of Jacob.

Ellicott denies that the list can be complete. Ten generations at least stand between Jacob and Joshua, so three between Jacob and Moses are scarcely possible, and the Israelites habitually built genealogies by dropping links, as the pedigrees of Ezra and of our Lord show. He reckons four or five names omitted between Kohath's son Amram and Moses' father Amram, and presses the numbers: Gershon had but two sons, Kohath four and Merari two, yet the Levites numbered twenty-two thousand three hundred males the year after the Exodus, an increase requiring some ten or eleven generations. Calvin takes the same fewness for the opposite proof. That three men so long-lived begat so few did not happen without design, so that in the fecundity which followed the miracle of grace might appear the clearer, God seeming first to mock their contemptible beginnings and then showing his power in their multiplication. He notes too what Amram's marriage cost the narrator: nature itself, before ever the law forbade it, dictated that a man should not take his aunt, who stands to him in a mother's degree, and Moses in confessing it proclaims his parents' disgrace for the glory of God — from which we learn that imitating the patriarchs indiscriminately is not safe.
17:
Whether Jochebed was Amram's aunt or his cousin is the one philological quarrel here. Gill holds for the aunt, since Numbers says expressly she was a daughter of Levi born in Egypt, though the Vulgate, Septuagint, Samaritan and Syriac all make her his uncle's daughter, as does Polyhistor after Demetrius. Clarke goes with the versions: the word is of uncertain force, Parkhurst showing it serves for an uncle and also for an uncle's son, the Vulgate elsewhere rendering it my paternal cousin — so the best critics suppose her a cousin-german and not an aunt. Ellicott needs no softening: marriages with aunts and nieces were not unlawful before the Law, and were common throughout the East and at Sparta.

The other names are noticed for what came of them. Gill thinks Izhar's sons named for Korah's sake, a remarkable history following in the next book, the other two being nowhere else named; Clarke observes that though Korah became a rebel, Moses in his impartiality set the name among his own progenitors; and Ellicott adds that Korah's sons did not share his sin and so did not die with him, but headed important families. On Elisheba, Clarke construes the name the oath of the Lord and makes her sister to Nahshon; Ellicott adds that Amminadab and Naashon stand among David's ancestors and so appear in the genealogies of our Lord, Naashon being prince of Judah at the Exodus; Wesley draws the rule that Levites might marry into any tribe, no confusion or loss of inheritance following. Of Putiel Gill canvasses three views — Lightfoot's, an Egyptian convert, perhaps of the stock of Potipherah among whom Joseph had sown true religion; the Targum of Jonathan and Jarchi, who make him Jethro; and Aben Ezra, whom he prefers, an Israelite whose name cannot now be explained.

On the emphatic naming, Gill reports the puzzle that Aaron stands first here and Moses first in the next verse: Aben Ezra accounts for it by Aaron's being the elder and prophesying in Egypt before his brother, though Moses was greater in dignity, so the true reason may be the writer's modesty; Jarchi thinks the reversal meant to show them equal; Gill allows the historian may simply not have cared, the point being to mark out the persons to future ages. Clarke makes the armies regularly arranged troops in battalions, and observes that God, having such under his care, bears the name Lord of hosts. Ellicott finds the term used of Israel here first, and refers it to the quasi-military organisation given during the struggle with Pharaoh, which let them leave Egypt not a disorderly mob but in array.

Calvin seizes the word for a contrast between the armies of a nation and two abject men who could never have borne so weighty a burden had God not worked through their hands beyond every hope. What was less probable, he asks, than that a multitude enough to make many nations should obey two men and migrate against a powerful king's will? What no earthly king could effect with all his terror, God did by two unwarlike men, one of whom kept deprecating the commission. Calvin notes an ambiguity in the closing verses, which might mean that God spoke in Midian and then in Egypt after some time elapsed, though he prefers to take the three together; Clarke would go further and begin the seventh chapter here, the sixth ending completely at the naming of the two. Gill treats the last verse as a bare repetition, the objection put as before — how should Pharaoh hearken to so mean a person and so poor a speaker, a king surrounded by wise counsellors and eloquent orators? Wesley answers from the charge itself: speak all that I say unto thee, as a faithful ambassador, for those who go on God's errand must not shun to declare his whole counsel.
